extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers and coastal/sea observers (members of the Royal Society, watermen, coastal observers) conducting tidal, marine, and mining observations (17th-century context)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical observational protocols, apparatus designs, and question-sets for measuring tides, sea properties, and surveying mines — intended to guide field observers (watermen, coastal observers) and natural philosophers in collecting systematic data over months and years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observations of spring tides (Dr. Wallis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dr. Wallis ... desires that some intelligent persons at London or Greenwich, but rather nearer the sea or upon the sea-shore, would make particular observations of all the spring tides, (new moon and full moon) between this and the end of November; and noting the hour and the perpendicular height; that it may be seen whether those in September or November be highest: And also to observe the low waters; which may be easily done by a mark made upon any standing post in the water, by any waterman or other intelligent person who dwells by the water side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observers should be located near the sea-shore; record date/time (hour) and perpendicular height for each spring tide (new and full moon) during the specified period; mark low water on a fixed standing post to measure low waters; use competent local observers (watermen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry into tidal increase/decrease proportions (Sir Robert Moray)
rubrics_metrics.description: It being observed, that tides increase and decrease regularly at several seasons according to the moon's age, ... It is wished that it may be inquired, in what proportion these increases and decreases, risings and fallings, happen to be in regard of one another?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether tidal height changes (from quarter moon to spring/neap etc.) follow a mathematical proportion (Moray suggests increases may be in the proportion of sines) and whether the increases before and after the middle correspond; make observations when wind or other accidents are absent to test the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for lengthy, location-focused observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Yet it is very desirable that observations be constantly made of all these particulars for some months and even years together. And because such observations will be the more easily and exactly made where the tides rise highest, it is presumed, that a fit apparatus being made for the purpose, they may be made about Bristol or Chepstow best of any places in England, because the tides are said thereabouts to rise to 10 or 12 fathoms; as upon the coast of Brittany in France, they do to 13 and 14.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan long-term observation campaigns (months to years) and preferentially choose locations where tidal ranges are large to increase measurement precision; equip such sites with suitable apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus design for measuring tidal rise/fall
rubrics_metrics.description: In some convenient place upon a wall, rock, or bridge, &c. let there be an observatory, standing as near as may be to the brink of the sea ... The observatory to be raised above the high water 18 or 20 feet; and a pump placed perpendicularly by the wall, reaching above the high water as high as conveniently may be. Upon the top of the pump a pulley to be fastened, for letting down into the pump a piece of floating wood, which, as the water comes in, may rise and fall with it. And because the rising and falling of the water amounts to 60 or 70 feet, the counterpoise of the weight that goes into the pump to hang upon as many pulleys as may serve to make it rise and fall within the space by which the height of the pump exceeds the height of the water; and because by this means the counterpoise will rise and fall slower, and consequently by less proportions than the weight itself, the first pulley may have upon it a wheel or two to turn indexes at any proportion required, so as to give the minute parts of the motion, and degrees of risings and fallings. All which is to be observed by pendulum watches that have minutes and seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct an observatory near the sea-brink raised ~18–20 ft above high water; install a vertical pump with floating wood attached to a pulley and counterpoise system with multiple pulleys to scale motion; include wheels to turn indexes to record small motion increments; time observations with pendulum watches showing minutes and seconds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing undulation in float measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent the water from rising and falling with an undulation, it will be proper that the hole by which the water enters be less than half the bore of the pump.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the inflow aperture smaller than half the pump bore to dampen undulatory motion and obtain steadier float readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record degrees of rising and falling every quarter hour
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. The degrees of rising and falling of the water every quarter of an hour, or as often as may be, from the periods of the tides and ebbs; to be observed night and day for two or three months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take frequent (every 15 minutes or as often as possible) measurements of water height during tidal cycles continuously day and night over a multi-month period to capture detailed rise/fall profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record water velocity at quarter-hour intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: 2. The degrees of the velocity of the motion of the water every quarter of an hour, for some whole tides together; to be observed by a second pendulum watch, and a log fastened to a line of about 50 fathoms wound about a wheel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure flow velocity at ~15-minute intervals across full tidal events using a second pendulum watch; use a log attached to ~50-fathom line wound on a wheel to quantify motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact measures of each highest tide and ebb over time
rubrics_metrics.description: 3. Exact measures of the heights of every highest tide and ebb, from one spring tide to another, for some months, or rather years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record peak high-water and low-water heights for each spring-to-spring interval across months/years to assess long-term variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record exact heights of spring tides and spring ebbs for years
rubrics_metrics.description: 4. The exact heights of spring tides and spring ebbs for some years together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a multi-year series of exact measurements for spring tides and corresponding ebbs to study interannual patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record wind direction, change times, and strength at each observation
rubrics_metrics.description: 5. The direction of the wind at every observation of the tides; the times of its changes, and the degrees of its strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At each tide observation, note wind direction, when it changes, and an estimate or measure of its strength; include these data to analyse wind influence on tides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record weather state and change times
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. The state of the weather as to rain, hail, mist, haziness, &c. and the times of its changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document prevailing weather conditions (rain, hail, mist, haze, etc.) and the timing of changes to correlate atmospheric conditions with tidal/sea observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record thermometric and barometric readings, hygroscope, and lunar/solar positions
rubrics_metrics.description: 7. At the times of observing the tides, the height of the thermometer, the baroscope, and the hygroscope; the age of the moon, and her azimuths and her place; also the sun's place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simultaneously record thermometer, barometer and hygroscope readings; note lunar age/azimuth/position and the sun's position for each tidal observation to support analysis of astronomical and meteorological influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patterns of tables for tide observations (Sir Rob. Moray)
rubrics_metrics.description: Of these patterns, one is for marking the precise time of high and low water during one month, that is between new and new moon, or full and full moon. The other for marking the degrees of the risings and fallings of the water in equal spaces of time, and the velocity of its motion at several heights; with the degrees of heat and cold, &c. these particulars having every one a ruled column allotted for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use two complementary table formats: (1) monthly high/low-water times (new–new or full–full); (2) time-series tables with columns for height increments in equal time steps, velocities at different heights, temperature, etc. Provide a ruled column for each measured variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea (Mr. Boyle) — salt proportion and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the proportion of salt in the water of different seas? Whether in the same sea it be always the same? If not, how does it differ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure salinity across different seas and over time at the same sea to determine spatial and temporal variability and factors influencing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea (Mr. Boyle) — relative gravity of sea waters
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the relative gravity of sea waters to fresh waters, and what to one another? Whether it varies not in summer and winter, and on other accounts? And whether in the same season its gravity proceeds only from the greater or less proportion of salt in it, and not sometimes from other causes? And what are the differing gravities of the sea water, according to the climates?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine specific gravities/densities of seawater vs. freshwater and among seas; test seasonal and climatic variation and assess whether variations are solely due to salinity or other causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea — sensory and compositional properties
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the odours, colours and tastes observable in sea water?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically record sensory properties (odor, color, taste) of seawater alongside chemical/physical measures to classify regional differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea — depth and seabed profile
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the depth of the sea in several places, and the order of its increase and decrease; and whether the bottom of the sea always rises towards the shore, unless accidentally interrupted?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map depths at multiple locations; determine typical bathymetric gradients toward shore and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea — seabed composition and differences from land surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the bottom of the sea, and how it differs from the surface of the earth, in reference to the soil, and evenness or roughness of the superficies; also the stones, minerals and vegetables to be found there?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and describe seabed samples (sediment, rocks, vegetation) and compare their composition and texture to terrestrial surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea — geographic figuration and communications
rubrics_metrics.description: What the figuration of the seas from north to south, and from east to west, and in the several hemispheres and climates? What communication there is of seas by straits and subterraneous conveyances?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chart large-scale sea configurations and investigate connections between basins (straits, possible subterranean conveyances) to understand circulation and exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea — motion by winds and depth of storms' effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the motion of the sea by winds, and how far storms reach downwards?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study wind-driven surface and subsurface motions, and measure vertical extent of storm influence on the water column.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea — grand motions, especially tides
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the grand motions of the body of the sea, especially of the tides, their nature and differences?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate large-scale water motions, focusing on mechanisms, spatial variability and types of tides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea — sea's chemical/biological effects
rubrics_metrics.description: What power the sea has to produce or hasten putrefaction in some bodies, and to preserve others; as wood, cables, &c. ? Of the power ascribed to the sea to eject dead bodies, succinum, ambergris ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test preservation vs. putrefaction effects of seawater on various materials and record instances and mechanisms of sea-mediated ejection of materials (biological remains, ambergris).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea — bioluminescence/shining at night
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the shining of the sea in the night?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and describe nocturnal sea luminescence occurrences, conditions, and possible causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning the sea — medical and agricultural virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: What are the medical virtues of the sea, especially against hydrophobia? What is its virtue to manure land? And what are the plants that thrive best with sea water?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimentally evaluate supposed medicinal properties (e.g., against hydrophobia) and agricultural uses of seawater; test which plants benefit from seawater exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiries concerning mines — six-head survey framework (Mr. Boyle)
rubrics_metrics.description: These queries are reduced by the author to six heads: I. The neighbouring country about the mines. II. The soil where the mines are. III. The signs of mines. IV. The structure and other particulars belonging to the mines themselves. V. The nature and circumstances of the ore. VI. The reduction of the ore into metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a structured six-part survey when investigating mines: describe surrounding country, soil type, surface/subsurface signs, mine structure and workings, ore character, and smelting/reduction methods. Each head is elaborated with many targeted subquestions (see subsequent rubric entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mines survey — Queries on the neighbouring country (Head I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the country be mountainous, plain, or distinguished with vales? Whether high or low, &c. fruitful or barren, cold or temperate, rocky or not, hollow or solid? Whether they run in ridges or seem confusedly placed; and, if the former, what way the ridges run north and south, &c. ... What it produces, and what it most abounds in? What cattle it nourishes, and what their nature and peculiarities? The diseases and lives of the inhabitants longer or shorter than ordinary? The rivers, brooks, springs, and other waters; and the nature of them? Whether the air be dry or moist, hot or cold, clear or foggy, thick or thin, heavy or light; any subterraneous streams, and what they are?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document topography, fertility, climate, vegetation/produce, livestock, epidemiology, hydrology, and atmospheric conditions around mines; note any subterranean streams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mines survey — The soil (Head II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the soil be stony; and, if it be, what kind of stones it abounds with? Whether it be clayey, marly, chalky, &c. ?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize soil types and rock occurrences at and near mining sites to aid prospecting and interpretation of subsurface geology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mines survey — Signs or indications of mines (Head III)
rubrics_metrics.description: By what signs they know or guess that there is a mine in such a place? Whether it be observed that trees and other greater plants seem to have their tops burned, or other leaves or outsides discoloured? Or whether there be any plants that affect to grow over such mines, or the contrary? What colour the stones and pebbles take in the brooks, springs, or other waters? — Whether the waters, by their taste, smell, ponderousness, &c. indicate any minerals? — Whether snow will not lie, or frost continue so long, or dew be collected upon the ground, more or less than usual? — And whether the dew or the rain there will discolour white linen or woollen cloths, spread over night on the surface of the ground? — The state of the place as to thunder and lightning, storms or earthquakes, nocturnal lights and fiery meteors? — What indications from mists, or the virgula divinatoria? — What signs afford a probability of mines, or direction for following a vein over hills, valleys, lakes, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record biotic, hydrologic, and surface anomalies (plant distress, discolored pebbles, unusual water taste/weight/odour, differential snow/frost/dew patterns, discolouration of cloth by rain/dew, unusual electrical or luminous phenomena, minerals indicated by mists) as prospecting indicators and for tracing veins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mines survey — Strata and surface indicators (part of Head III)
rubrics_metrics.description: The strata under the surface: their number, nature, depth, order, thickness, &c. — Indications by certain stones or marcasites, &c. — Peculiar kind of earths. Also heats or damps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the sequence, thickness and nature of subsurface strata, presence of indicator minerals, peculiar soils, and occurrences of heat/dampness as diagnostic features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mines survey — Structure and working particulars (Head IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: The depth of the shaft or grove: what its width and extent? Whether the vein run horizontal or dip? what inclination it has? What its flexures; and what its directions? — What air-shaft belongs to the mine? Whether it be single, double, &c. and if several, what their distances, situation, &c.? — What waters spring in the mine; at what depths; and their quantity and nature? — What expedients and engines are employed to free the mines from water? — What are the conditions, number, &c. of the adits? — Whether the mine be troubled with damps, and of what kind they are? — What methods the mine men use in following the vein and tracing their passages under ground ... ? — How the miners deal with the rocks and spars they often meet with before they come at the ore? Whether they use fire to soften, calcine, or crack them? ... What instruments they use to break the rock, &c.? And how the mine men work; whether naked or clothed? And what lights they use to work by? — How veins are followed, lost, and recovered? And how several miners work on the same vein? And what is the best way of getting all the ore in a vein and most conveniently? — How they convey out their ore and other things that are to be carried out of the mine?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record mine geometry (shaft depth/width, vein orientation/inclination/flexures), ventilation (air-shafts), groundwater occurrences and drainage methods, adit conditions, gas/damp hazards, tunnelling/following practices, rock-breaking techniques (including use of fire), tools, working conditions (clothing, lighting), vein recovery strategies, and ore haulage methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mines survey — Nature and characteristics of the ore (Head V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the ore runs in the vein, or lies dispersed in scattered pieces; or be divided partly into a vein, and partly into loose masses; or like a wall between two rocks, as it were in a cleft; or be interspersed in the firm rock, like speckled marble? Or be found in grains like sand or gravel; as store of excellent tin is said to be found in some parts of Cornwall at the sides and in the channels of running waters; or whether the ore be of a softer consistence, like earth or loam, as there is lead-ore in Ireland holding store of silver; and iron ore in the north parts of Scotland and elsewhere? And what is observable in it as to weight, colour, mixture, &c. Whether any part of the metal be found in the mine perfect and complete?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe ore occurrence mode (vein, nodules, disseminated, seam), grain size and consistency (e.g., sand-like, loam-like), physical properties (weight, color, associations/mixtures) and whether native metal occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mines survey — Reduction of ore into metal (Head VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: VI. The reduction of the ore into metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe local metallurgical processes used to reduce the ore to metal, furnaces, fluxes, yields, and efficiencies; document traditional and technical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method to find the Year of the Julian Period (M. J. De Billy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply the solar cycle by 4845, and the lunar by 4200, and that of the indiction by 6916. Then divide the sum of the products by 7980, which is the Julian period: the remainder of the division, without having regard to the quotient, will be the year required. Ex. gr. ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: compute products of cycle numbers with specified multipliers (solar×4845, lunar×4200, indiction×6916), sum them, divide by 7980, and take the remainder as the Julian period year; example given for illustration.
